must_remember: Physical quantities are classified into scalars (rank zero), vectors (rank one), and tensors of higher ranks.
Polar vectors reverse sign under spatial inversion ($mathbf{r} \rightarrow -mathbf{r}$), whereas axial vectors retain their sign.
The scalar dot product yields a scalar ($A B \cos(\theta)$), while the vector cross product yields an axial vector perpendicular to both operands.
Direction cosines satisfy the identity $l^2 + m^2 + n^2 = 1$ where $l = \cos(\alpha)$, $m = \cos(\beta)$, and $n = \cos(\gamma)$.
Angular momentum ($mathbf{L} = mathbf{r} \times mathbf{p}$) and torque ($\boldsymbol{\tau} = mathbf{r} \times mathbf{F}$) are classic examples of axial vectors.

glossary.meaning: A vector representing linear translation that reverses direction under spatial inversion (parity transformation).
A vector representing rotational characteristics associated with an axis that does not invert its direction under spatial inversion.
Cosines of the angles made by a vector with the respective Cartesian coordinate axes, denoted by $l$, $m$, and $n$.
An apparent inertial force given by $mathbf{F}_{cor} = -2m (\boldsymbol{omega} \times mathbf{v}_r)$ experienced in a rotating reference frame.
